questions.question: Q: What is the Aeneid about and who wrote it?
questions.correctAnswer: An epic poem by Virgil (29-19 BC) telling how the Trojan hero Aeneas fled Troy, wandered the Mediterranean, and reached Italy to found the Roman race. It explores themes of pietas, fate, and the cost of empire.

questions.question: Q: What are the Metamorphoses and what is distinctive about Ovid's approach?
questions.correctAnswer: Ovid's long narrative poem (AD 8) collecting myths of transformation. Ovid is distinctive for his wit, irony, playful subversion of epic conventions, and sympathetic portrayal of the victims of power.

questions.question: Q: Who was Catullus and what is his poetry about?
questions.correctAnswer: Catullus (c.84-54 BC) was a Roman lyric poet whose work covers passionate love (poems to Lesbia), friendship, political invective, and social commentary.

questions.question: Q: How does the Aeneid reflect Augustan ideology?
questions.correctAnswer: The Aeneid celebrates Rome's destiny and Augustus's rule by showing Aeneas as the ideal Roman who sacrifices personal happiness for duty. However, Virgil also shows the human cost of this destiny.

questions.question: Q: What is the significance of Ovid's exile?
questions.correctAnswer: Ovid was exiled by Augustus in AD 8, partly because of the Metamorphoses and Ars Amatoria. His exile suggests his poetry was seen as politically subversive.

questions.question: Q: How often do verse set texts change?
questions.correctAnswer: Every two years. You must check your exam board's specification for the current prescribed texts for your year of examination.

questions.question: Q: What is the typical metre of epic poetry?
questions.correctAnswer: Dactylic hexameter: six feet per line, each foot being a dactyl (- uu) or spondee (--). This is the metre of the Aeneid and Metamorphoses.

questions.question: Q: Name the four most common verse authors studied at GCSE Latin.
questions.correctAnswer: Virgil (Aeneid), Ovid (Metamorphoses), Catullus (lyric poems), and Horace (Odes).

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Compare how Virgil and Ovid approach the theme of power in their verse set texts. (8 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Virgil and Ovid both engage with the theme of power but from very different perspectives. Virgil's Aeneid presents power as a divine imperative: Aeneas must fulfil his fate (fatum) to found Rome, ordained by Jupiter. Power is legitimate when exercised in service of Rome's destined future, and Aeneas's pietas demands he subordinate personal desires to this mission. However, Virgil does not present this uncritically: Dido's death shows the devastating human cost of imperial destiny, and Aeneas's final killing of Turnus in rage raises questions about whether power corrupts even the most dutiful hero. Ovid's Metamorphoses is far more sceptical. The gods repeatedly abuse their power to exploit mortals: Jupiter pursues Io, Europa, and Callisto; Apollo pursues Daphne; and divine power is shown as arbitrary, selfish, and destructive. Where Virgil's gods direct fate for Rome's glory, Ovid's gods act from personal desire. Ovid also shows transformation itself as an exercise of power, stripping mortals of agency. This can be read as a subtle critique of Augustus, who 'transformed' Rome from Republic to Empire. Where Virgil legitimises power through destiny, Ovid exposes its cruelty and self-interest.
